newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda sees concern over high arabica coffee price.
newsitem.headline: Uganda sees concern over high arabica coffee price.

text.p: Ugandan coffee authorities said on Tuesday producers were concerned about runaway arabica coffee prices and growing margins between arabicas and robustas.

William Naggaga, board secretary of the main policy body, the Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA), told Reuters producers were impressed by the trends in coffee prices but concerned about the widening margin between the different types.
Naggaga said an extraordinary meeting of the technical group of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in London on Thursday would address arabica prices.
"The purpose of the meeting is to look at the escalation of arabica prices which are causing a lot of concern and might affect consumption of coffee negatively," he said.

A similar price rise occurred in November 1994, causing a slight drop in coffee consumption as people switched to cheaper beverages, and Naggaga said: "What we're concerned about is to ensure that we don't jeopardise the demand aspect."

Prices of arabicas -- used for ground coffee -- approximately doubled between early December 1996 and early March this year. At the same time robustas -- used mainly in instant coffee -- rose only by some 50 percent.

On Monday, though, arabica futures in New York fell sharply to a 2-1/2 week low as supply worries eased. The May futures contract ended down 17.70 cents a lb at 168.65, compared with a high of 209.50 cents on March 5.

Ugandan coffee authorities also confirmed they were cutting exports by around 200,000 bags in line with a decision reached at a meeting earlier this month of the Abidjan-based InterAfrica Coffee Organisation (IACO).
But Naggaga said a drop in exports did not mean a drop in production.

The worst weather for Uganda in a decade would have a negative, but not significant, impact on output, and an outbreak of coffee wilt disease (tracheomycosis) -- which has affected 11 growing districts -- would have a limited impact on the 1996/97 crop, he said.
"We have a team now out in the field assessing the wilt situation but it is not likely to affect the production levels (this year) in any significant way," Naggaga said.
The IACO gathering agreed to cut robustas available to the world market by 850,000 bags in the first half of calendar 1997.

"The bags are to be distributed internally among the African producers. Uganda's exports for that period will hence be reduced by approximately 200,000 bags," Naggaga said in a letter to UCDA board members seen by Reuters on Tuesday.
The March 6-7 IACO meeting in Abidjan was chaired by Abel Rwendeire, IACO vice-chairman and Uganda's minister of state for trade and industry.

Naggaga told Reuters the cut in exports meant Uganda's exports would be around 4.0 million bags in 1996/97 instead of a forecast of 4.25 million bags sent to the International Coffee Organisation (ICO).
"Our projection (for 1996/97 exports) had been about 4.25 million bags but with a reduction we shall come to about 4.0 million bags or slightly under that," he said.
At the meeting in Abidjan Uganda agreed to an allocation of 21.96 percent of the overall export cut of 850,000 60-kg bags.
